history.heading: Ancient Bengal
paragraphs: Bangladesh occupies most of the Bengal delta, formed by the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers. The fertile region supported early urban centres such as Mahasthangarh and was part of empires including the Mauryas and Guptas. The Buddhist Pala dynasty (8th–12th centuries) built great monasteries such as Paharpur, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Islam spread from the 13th century, especially among the rural population. Bengal became an independent sultanate and later a wealthy province of the Mughal Empire, famous for its fine muslin cloth.

history.heading: British rule and Partition
paragraphs: The British East India Company took control of Bengal after the Battle of Plassey in 1757. Colonial policies contributed to devastating famines in 1770 and 1943. Bengal was a centre of cultural renaissance and anti-colonial nationalism.
At the Partition of India in 1947, Muslim-majority East Bengal became East Pakistan, part of Pakistan but separated from West Pakistan by 1,600 km of Indian territory.

history.heading: Language movement and liberation
paragraphs: When Pakistan's government tried to make Urdu the sole national language, Bengalis protested; police killed several student demonstrators in Dhaka on 21 February 1952. This day is now commemorated worldwide as International Mother Language Day.

Political and economic discrimination fuelled demands for autonomy, led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. After his party won the 1970 elections but was denied power, the Pakistani army launched a brutal crackdown in March 1971. In the Liberation War that followed, hundreds of thousands to possibly millions of people were killed and about 10 million fled to India. With Indian intervention, Bangladesh won independence on 16 December 1971.

history.heading: Independent Bangladesh
paragraphs: Sheikh Mujib was assassinated in 1975, and a period of military rule followed. Democracy was restored in 1991, after which power alternated between the Awami League, led by Sheikh Hasina, and the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), led by Khaleda Zia.

Sheikh Hasina governed from 2009 with increasing authoritarianism until student-led mass protests in July and August 2024, in which hundreds were killed, forced her to resign and flee to India. An interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus oversaw reforms before general elections in February 2026.

culture.heading: Language and literature
paragraphs: Bengali (Bangla) is the national language and a deep source of identity. Rabindranath Tagore, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, wrote the national anthem, Amar Shonar Bangla, and Kazi Nazrul Islam, the "rebel poet", is the national poet.
About 90 percent of Bangladeshis are Muslim, with a significant Hindu minority and smaller Buddhist and Christian communities, including indigenous peoples of the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

culture.heading: Festivals and arts
paragraphs: Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year in April, is celebrated with colourful processions. Religious festivals include Eid and Durga Puja. Baul music, sung by wandering mystic minstrels, is recognised by UNESCO, and jamdani weaving produces fine patterned muslin.
Rickshaw art, the colourful painted decoration of cycle rickshaws, is a distinctive folk art of Dhaka.

culture.heading: Food and sport
paragraphs: Rice and fish are the heart of Bangladeshi cuisine; hilsa (ilish) is the national fish. Dishes include biryani, bhuna khichuri, pitha (rice cakes) and many sweets such as roshogolla and mishti doi.
Cricket is by far the most popular sport, and the national team has become competitive at the international level.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Bangladesh is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government, while the president, elected by parliament, is head of state. The unicameral parliament, the Jatiya Sangsad, has 300 directly elected seats plus seats reserved for women.

Politics has long been polarised between the Awami League and the BNP, with frequent strikes, violence and disputed elections. After the 2024 uprising, the Awami League's activities were banned, and debates focused on constitutional reform, accountability for abuses and the role of Islamist parties.

politics.heading: Foreign relations
paragraphs: Bangladesh balances relations with India, China and the United States. Since 2017 it has hosted around a million Rohingya refugees who fled violence in Myanmar, mostly in camps near Cox's Bazar. It is one of the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping.

economy.heading: From poverty to growth
paragraphs: Once described as a "basket case", Bangladesh has achieved strong growth and large reductions in poverty since the 1990s. It is set to graduate from the UN's least developed country category in 2026.

The ready-made garment industry is the engine of the economy, making Bangladesh the world's second-largest clothing exporter after China and employing millions of workers, mainly women. The 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse, which killed over 1,100 people, led to safety reforms.

economy.heading: Other pillars and challenges
paragraphs: Remittances from millions of Bangladeshis working abroad, especially in the Gulf, are vital. Agriculture remains important, with rice, jute and fish. Microcredit, pioneered by Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank, became influential worldwide. The currency is the taka.

Bangladesh is one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change, facing cyclones, floods and rising sea levels across its low-lying delta. Other challenges include corruption, banking sector weakness and dependence on a single export industry.
